What do you laser experts think of this post of Frank's?

[http://comac.enter.net/webhf/371860949.html](http://comac.enter.net/webhf/371860949.html)

> (I never turn my lasers off, they run 24 hours a day. My HeNe has been turned on and running for nearly 10 years now (replaced my Spectra-Physics 124B Stabilite in 1995) . . . that's 87,600 hours. Yes, that isn't a typo. See the secret to long laser life now? ... It's the thermal expansion and contraction that eventually kills them. Actually, the thermal expansion and contraction is a precursor to the dropping of pressure within the tube. Hard sealing helped this to a great degree -- but it's not perfect. You see, your HeNe gas (only a few molecules) leaves the tube as it reaches thermal stability (turning on) -- then stops when thermal stability is achieved. Outside air enters when during contraction (turning off) and then stops when thermal stability (room temperature) is achived. That is why getters become contaminated. This doesn't happen when the laser remains on. And it is also why I have 87,600 hours on my HeNe. For the pennies in electricity this costs, the savings far exceed the cost of a new gas laser system. Plus, it's not "dying" a slow death over time

Leaving aside the commentary on spaghetti from the full text in the link (which is making me hungry as I wait at work for a DVD to burn at 1am) is there anything to the idea that leaving the laser on all the time will keep it running longer?

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
From Sam's Laser Faq, HeNe section

[http://www.repairfaq.org/sam/laserhen.htm#henhlt](http://www.repairfaq.org/sam/laserhen.htm#henhlt)

quote:

"(From: Lynn Strickland ([stricks760@earthlink.net](mailto:stricks760@earthlink.net)).)

Typical failure mechanism in a HeNe is cathode sputtering -- seldom gas leakage in the newer (like since 1983) tubes. Shelf life is stated to be about 10 years, but it's not uncommon at all to see HeNe lasers built in the early 1980's that still meet full spec.

Interesting lifetime note - it used to be that you left a HeNe 'on' at all times to prolong life. Since hard-sealing, you should turn it off while not in use. If it's a 20,000 hour tube, and you only turn it on for a few hundred hours a year, it will last a heck of a long time. Not uncommon at all for the HeNe to outlive several power supplies. The larger diameter tubes tend to last longer, but it also depends on fill pressure and operating current (higher fill-pressure tubes last longer). The typical 5 mW red HeNe will commonly live to 40k to 50k operating hours.

As for cathode sputtering, the tube has an aluminum cathode that is 'pickled' during the production process to add a layer of oxidation about 200 microns thick. The oxidation layer prevents aluminum from being bombarded away from the cathode during plasma discharge. As the tube ages, the oxide layer is depleted until aluminum is exposed. Sputtered aluminum can stick to the mirror, causing power decline, or to the inside of the glass envelope, causing the discharge to arc internally. This arcing, if allowed to continue for a period of time, will also cook the power supply. A tube with no oxidation layer on the cathode will die in about 200 hours of use. OR, once the oxidation layer is depleted, the tube will die in about 200 hours. This is why a HeNe life curve is usually pretty flat, then quickly degrading to nothing over about a 200 hour period.

"

I'm a little confused. How can He leak out of a tube which is at a very much lower pressure than the atmosphere around it? If the turn-on and/or turn-off environment is the cause of gas pressure or mixture changes, what's the failure mechanism that limits the laser's shelf life? 

From my experience processing CO2 and He-Cd laser tubes, I recall that the pressure in the tube controlled the electrical properties (voltage needed to start the tube, current needed for optimum output power), and gas mixture determined the maximum output power. Since the output power of most He-Nes stays relatively constant untill the end of their lives (except in the presence of contamination of the optics), I believe the gas inside the tube stays pretty much the same over the laser's lifetime.

The cathode sputtering mechanism of failure seems most plausible to me.

BobH says:

I'm a little confused. How can He leak out of a tube which is at a very much lower pressure than the atmosphere around it? 

This is a semi-permeable membrane phenomenon which does'nt follow ordinary gas pressure laws. So in theory over time the very low pressure inside the laser tube goes down still further as the major constituent He passes by random processes through the glass and cant be replaced unless there is a very Helium rich atmosphere outside that randomly causes He atoms to wander back inside the tube. 

It is seen more familiarly in osmotic pressure demos where small salt ions and water molecules pass through a semipermeable membrane in a solution but large molecules cant get through the membrane and this creates a pressure difference.

Quantum tunnelling? I'm joking! I'm joking!

[quote:7bbe2346b6]I thought it was the He that did "the metastable state for population inversion" Dinesh. [/quote:7bbe2346b6]

I'll take your word for it, Jeff. I haven't looked at a level diagram for HeNe in years! I always thought of it as: "up to He and down to Ne" Under this method, it should be called NeHe, perhaps?

I get the feeling that what Frank seems to be saying is that when the laser is turning on, there is an expansion due to heating. This expansion causes some kind of "pushing" mechanism which "pushes" the He out of the tube. When the laser is turned off, there is a shrinkage due to the cooling. This causes some kind of "sucking" mechanism which pulls the air into the tube. Besides not knowing of any such mechanism, I did some back-of-an-envelope calculations for velocity of He in both cases. Using

(1/2)*m*(v^2) = (3/2)*k*T

where k = Boltzmann's constant

T = temperature

m = mass

If you assume that the plasma in the tube is about 60C, reasonable I think since the water for cooling Argons does not boil or steam and I've got to think that 10mW HeNe doesn't run as hot as a 5W Argon, and the mass of a He molecule is 4*1.6*((10^(-27)) kg (mass of a proton), then

velocity of He with laser off ~ 1375 m/s

velocity of He with laser on ~ 1477 m/s

Ratio,

vel of He (laser off)/vel of He (laser on) ~ 1375/1477 ~ 0.93

It would appear that the velocity of the He is pretty much the same. I also did some calculations on expansion due to the laser being on and hot (again, using 60C). It turned out that the volume inside the tube expands by about 2% or so. Not enough to cause significant loss due to any "pushing" or "pulling" action.

As for the osmosis, I seem to remember from my A level Chemistry (a l-o-o-ng time ago!) that osmotic pressure depended only on differences in molecular weight and density of the same molecule. I'm thinking particularly of the trick we used to do as schoolkids where you get amoeba in a dish of water and then salt the water. In fact, the conventional wisdom I was told was to never keep the laser off for too long because of osmoosis. When the laser is on, the plasma circulates the components and there is no consistent pressure on the sides of the tube, but when the laser is off there is such a constant pressure and the osmosis loss is greater. But I can't think there's any great difference in osmosis that depends on whether the laser is on or off

Maybe it's entanglement!

theta = (inv)sin(0.04/d)

Actually, my feeling is that Frank seems to think that there is loss due to on-off transitions, as opposed to steady state. That I feel is wrong. In fact I was told it's a bad idea to leave your laser off for too long precisely because osmosis would cause loss of material in the tube.
